24:00 There are 4 models. V3-base (pretrained), V3 (simple fine tuned SFT), R1-zero (reinforcement learning trained but without human chain-of-thought data also called cold start), R1 (same as R1-zero but with human COT bootstrap data). They say R1 is better than R1-zero because R1-zero's thought process was not clean and mixed Chinese and English languages.

The GRPO basically says given a question, produce lets say 5 thought process + final solutions to it. For all solutions which are correct, we increase the probability of the model to generate the same thought process in the future, and for all the ones it got wrong, we suppress the probabilities. We use 5 samples for a mean and standard deviation, to not distort it too much. Also, we rubber band it to a reference model to prevent the RL from pushing it too far away.

When we say R1 was trained with data generated by V3, it is probably talking about the RL process, where the model thinks and its probabilities are upshifted and downshifted.
When we say V3 was trained on R1 (which I don't remember reading in the paper, but it is possible) it could mean distillation. When, we train V3 on R1's outputs it gives V3 the knowledge of R1. Whatever extra knowledge R1 earned from the RL process is imparted back to V3. 

Personally, I think just because a model does great on popular benchmarks, doesn't mean it would also be economically useful. OpenAI models are larger and more expensive because they can do a lot more than just this one benchmark. You need a bigger brain to do everything.

The insistence of the US to treat this as an arms race and be openly hostile to China and others is literally putting us on a trajectory for some sort of dystopian outcome. My thoughts:

The Risk of National AI Competition

Current U.S. policy regarding AI development is built upon a dangerous premise: the idea that we must restrict other nations' access to AI technology to maintain technological superiority. This approach manifests most visibly in semiconductor export controls and technology sanctions, particularly targeted at China. However, this strategy is both ethically unconscionable and pragmatically misguided.
Consider China, a nation of over one billion people that U.S. policy treats as a monolithic entity with uniform values and intentions. This framing fundamentally misunderstands the nature of human societies. It's absurd to claim that we can meaningfully characterize the aggregate values and ideologies of such a vast and diverse population. Within China, as in any nation, there exists a rich tapestry of individual beliefs, values, and aspirations - many of which likely align closely with those held by people in the West.

The Moral Imperative of Shared Progress

When we prevent nations from accessing AI technology, we're not simply opposing a government or an ideology - we're denying hundreds of millions (or billions in the case of China) of individual human beings access to potentially transformative technologies. According to leading AI researchers, these technologies have the potential to dramatically reduce human suffering and improve quality of life on an unprecedented scale. Deliberately withholding such technology from any portion of humanity is ethically indefensible. A nation who pursues such restrictions against other nations can make no claims that it believes in anything that resembles “human rights.” I can think of nothing more inhumane.

The Dangers of an AI Arms Race

History has shown that technological arms races rarely end well for anyone involved. In the context of AI, the stakes are even higher. If nations pursue AI development in a competitive, adversarial manner, we risk creating a world where vast power imbalances become entrenched and immutable. The concentration of AI capabilities in the hands of a select few - whether they be tech corporations or government entities - poses grave risks to global stability and human welfare.
